main.title: Drakan: The Ancients' Gates
main.subtitle: A warrior and a dragon share the journey
main.summary: Drakan: The Ancients' Gates is Surreal Software's PlayStation 2 action-adventure, first released in North America on 29 January 2002. Rynn and the dragon Arokh continue the partnership introduced in Drakan: Order of the Flame, travelling through a fantasy world on foot and in the air. The two scales give the adventure its shape. A fortress can be a place to approach through its doors or a landmark seen from above. The player moves between Rynn's immediate struggle with enemies and the wider freedom offered by a dragon in flight.

cards.heading: A warrior and a dragon share the journey
cards.text: Drakan: The Ancients' Gates is Surreal Software's PlayStation 2 action-adventure, first released in North America on 29 January 2002. Rynn and the dragon Arokh continue the partnership introduced in Drakan: Order of the Flame, travelling through a fantasy world on foot and in the air. The two scales give the adventure its shape. A fortress can be a place to approach through its doors or a landmark seen from above. The player moves between Rynn's immediate struggle with enemies and the wider freedom offered by a dragon in flight.

cards.heading: Fight on the ground, then take to the air
cards.text: Rynn uses weapons and magic during the on-foot sections, with a target lock helping keep attention on a particular enemy. Spells are performed through directional inputs, making their use another activity to learn alongside movement and attacks. Shops and discoveries provide equipment for later encounters. Arokh changes the pace through flight and aerial combat, opening routes that belong to a different scale of the landscape. Returning to the ground makes those large spaces tangible again, connecting the view from the sky to the passages and opponents waiting below.

cards.heading: A PC adventure finds a console continuation
cards.text: The original Drakan appeared on Windows in 1999, while The Ancients' Gates continued the world exclusively on PlayStation 2. Alan Patmore led the design, with Erik Aho composing its music. The sequel retained the partnership at the centre of the earlier game while expanding Rynn's equipment and magical abilities. PAL editions followed in July 2002. Its distinctive pleasure is the connection between the two protagonists: the dragon is more than a distant story companion because flying with Arokh becomes a regular way of inhabiting the same world Rynn explores on foot.

main.title: Space Channel 5: Part 2
main.summary: Ulala answers kidnappers with matching steps, instrument duels and a growing crowd of rescued dancers.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Space Channel 5: Part 2 is United Game Artists' 2002 rhythm game, originally released in Japan for Dreamcast and PlayStation 2. Reporter Ulala investigates another outbreak of forced dancing and kidnappings. The sequel develops the first game's imitation battles into a musical broadcast, with new opponents, instrument contests and a soundtrack credited to Wave Master musicians.

cards.heading: Listen, remember, answer
cards.text: An opponent performs a phrase, and Ulala must repeat its directions and timing. Remembering the order is only part of the task: a pause or a held call matters as much as the next step. The player listens for the shape of the phrase, then answers when the performance passes to Ulala. A small set of inputs leaves room for increasingly elaborate patterns, turning attention to rhythm rather than a growing list of moves.

cards.heading: A rhythm becomes an instrument
cards.text: Instrument battles give that exchange another voice. A sequence can become a musical reply, while other encounters introduce sung phrases or ask Ulala to distinguish targets as they appear. The basic act of listening and answering survives those changes, but its presentation keeps shifting with the scene. A successful response feels like a contribution to the number being performed, carrying the player from following a pattern into taking part in the music.

cards.heading: The report gathers a crowd
cards.text: Rescued people join Ulala's procession, so progress changes the group moving through the report. A confrontation starts with a few performers and grows into a larger dance as more people are freed. Returning characters such as Pudding and Space Michael give the broadcast other personalities to play against. That expanding company makes success visible in the scene itself: the player continues through the story accompanied by the people their earlier answers have brought along.

main.title: Jet Set Radio Future
main.subtitle: Making the city your own
main.summary: Jet Set Radio Future is Smilebit's skating and graffiti game for Xbox, released in 2002. The GG crew crosses a stylised Tokyo, marking its territory while rival gangs and the Rokkaku Group stand in the way. Rails, rooftops and walls turn the city into a network of routes to discover.

cards.heading: Tokyo on skates
cards.text: Jet Set Radio Future is Smilebit's skating and graffiti game for Xbox, released in 2002. The GG crew crosses a stylised Tokyo, marking its territory while rival gangs and the Rokkaku Group stand in the way. Rails, rooftops and walls turn the city into a network of routes to discover.

cards.heading: A line through the streets
cards.text: Jump onto a railing to grind, then link tricks before leaping towards the next ledge. Billboards offer brief wallrides that can carry a skater higher. A boost spends ten spray cans for a burst of speed, so the paint collected along the way also helps reach the next part of a route.

cards.heading: Paint in motion
cards.text: Graffiti appears at marked spots, with larger designs spread across several targets. Holding the spray trigger fills them as the skater passes. Finding a path that reaches every mark becomes part of learning each district. Rival encounters and police battles interrupt the journey, asking the crew to turn the same movement skills towards an opponent.

cards.heading: Back at the Garage
cards.text: The Garage gives the GG crew a place to regroup. Talking to its members supplies hints, while Roboy offers practice and a graffiti editor. New designs can be taken back into the streets. Professor K's pirate radio accompanies the action, joining the city's visual identity to a soundtrack built around beats, samples and vocals.

main.title: Onimusha 2: Samurai's Destiny
main.summary: Onimusha 2: Samurai's Destiny, released in Japan as Onimusha 2, is a 2002 action-adventure game developed and released by Capcom for the PlayStation 2.

cards.heading: Onimusha 2: Samurai's Destiny
cards.text: Onimusha 2: Samurai's Destiny, released in Japan as Onimusha 2, is a 2002 action-adventure game developed and released by Capcom for the PlayStation 2. It is the second installment in the Onimusha series and was released in March 2002. Set in medieval Japan, the plot revolves around a new protagonist, Jubei Yagyu, who is on a quest of revenge as he battles a demon army led by Nobunaga Oda, a sinister warlord who eliminated the Yagyu clan. Across his quest, Jubei learns of his oni heritage which grants him powers to slay the demons and meets new allies who also wish to defeat Nobunaga and his army of Genma.

cards.heading: Allies open different paths
cards.text: The game retains the action elements from its predecessor such as the use of multiple special weapons that can be upgraded with souls collected from defeated enemies. Apart from the main character, the game features four playable sub-characters, each of whom shares a part in the story. The player's actions determine which characters will decide to help Jubei in his quest. These characters were added by the Capcom staff to give a bigger depth to the game and expand the game's feeling of adventure. Each character that the player befriends will have different cutscenes as well as personal story arcs that Jubei gets to experience, although the main narrative will largely remain the same. There are certain characters or cutscenes that cannot be experienced on the same playthrough, due to plot reasons.

cards.heading: Branching stories and familiar action
cards.text: Publications for video games generally praised Onimusha 2 for its branching storyline paths, music, re-playability, and for keeping the action elements from its predecessor and adding new gameplay elements, although the game was criticized for abandoning its RPG element about 40% of the way through and for its similarity to the original game. Also, the American release did not contain the Japanese audio unlike the first game. The graphics and the CGI intro were highly praised.

main.title: Resident Evil
main.summary: Resident Evil is a 2002 survival horror game developed and published by Capcom for the GameCube.

cards.heading: Resident Evil
cards.text: Resident Evil is a 2002 survival horror game developed and published by Capcom for the GameCube. It is a remake of the 1996 PlayStation game Resident Evil, the first installment in the Resident Evil video game series. The story takes place in 1998 near the fictional Midwestern town of Raccoon City where a series of bizarre murders have taken place. The player takes on the role of either Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine, S.T.A.R.S. officers sent in by the city and the R.P.D. to investigate the murders.

cards.heading: Rebuilding the mansion on GameCube
cards.text: Resident Evil was developed over the course of fourteen months as part of an exclusivity deal between Capcom and Nintendo for the series in their Capcom Five partnership. It was directed by Shinji Mikami, who also designed and directed the original Resident Evil. Mikami decided to produce a remake because he felt that the original had not aged well enough and that the GameCube's capabilities could bring it closer to his original vision. The game retains the same graphical presentation, with 3D models superimposed over pre-rendered backgrounds. However, the quality of the graphics was vastly improved. The remake also features new gameplay mechanics, revised puzzles, additional explorable areas, a revised script, and new story details including an entire subplot cut from the original game.

cards.heading: Reception and the HD remaster
cards.text: Upon release, Resident Evil received acclaim from video game journalists, who praised its graphics and improved gameplay over the original game. It is often described as one of the best, scariest, and most visually impressive entries in the Resident Evil series. However, the game sold worse than expected, leading Capcom to change the direction of the series to a more action-oriented approach. In 2008, the game was ported to the Wii, featuring a new control system. In 2015, a high-definition remaster was released to critical and commercial success for PlayStation 3, PlayStation 4, Windows, Xbox 360, and Xbox One, then later for Nintendo Switch in 2019. Retrospectively, critics and fans regard Resident Evil as one of the greatest game remakes ever made.

main.title: Kingdom Hearts
main.subtitle: Disney and Square Discover a World in Common
main.summary: Kingdom Hearts brought an original travelling party into Disney worlds and made that unlikely meeting the basis of a new series.

cards.heading: An unusual partnership
cards.text: Kingdom Hearts first released in Japan for PlayStation 2 on 28 March 2002. The collaboration between Square and Disney brought Sora, an original young protagonist, together with Donald Duck and Goofy. The familiar characters were companions in a continuing adventure rather than a collection of unrelated guest appearances.

cards.heading: A travelling party crosses familiar worlds
cards.text: Their journey moves through Disney worlds threatened by the Heartless. Sora's Keyblade connects that travelling party to the larger conflict. Recognisable characters and places provide an entry into a story that also asks the player to follow new relationships, so prior familiarity with Disney is useful without explaining everything in advance.

cards.heading: The beginning, before the collections
cards.text: The first game later appeared within collections and on other platforms. Those packages bring different points in the series together, but the original 2002 release was its starting point. Looking back from the many sequels makes the initial proposition strikingly simple: three unlikely companions have to travel together.

cards.heading: Traveling between worlds in the Gummi Ship
cards.text: The Gummi Ship connects the worlds through rail-shooting routes. Players steer from behind the vessel, avoiding obstacles and firing at enemy ships. New weapons, engines and armour expand its customisation, while blueprints offer ready-made designs. Later, Warp Drive lets Sora return instantly to previously visited worlds; new destinations still require surviving their route first.

main.title: Fire Emblem: The Binding Blade
main.subtitle: Roy leads an army across Elibe
main.summary: Fire Emblem: The Binding Blade is Intelligent Systems' Game Boy Advance tactical role-playing game following Roy and his growing army through a war in Elibe. Story scenes introduce the next conflict before the player moves individual soldiers across a grid-based battlefield. The first handheld entry in the series also gave Roy an adventure of his own after his appearance in Super Smash Bros. Melee. Its campaign depends on developing a particular group of characters, making the outcome of a map important both to the wider story and to the people available for the next battle.

cards.heading: Roy leads an army across Elibe
cards.text: Fire Emblem: The Binding Blade is Intelligent Systems' Game Boy Advance tactical role-playing game following Roy and his growing army through a war in Elibe. Story scenes introduce the next conflict before the player moves individual soldiers across a grid-based battlefield. The first handheld entry in the series also gave Roy an adventure of his own after his appearance in Super Smash Bros. Melee. Its campaign depends on developing a particular group of characters, making the outcome of a map important both to the wider story and to the people available for the next battle.

cards.heading: A weapon changes the encounter
cards.text: Units have different weapons, movement ranges and responsibilities, requiring the player to consider which opponent each character should face. The weapon triangle gives axes, lances and swords advantages over one another, adding another relationship to the choice of position. Equipment also has a limited number of uses, so preparing an attack involves the condition of the weapon as well as the strength of its bearer. A successful turn coordinates several decisions, placing one unit where it can contribute without leaving another exposed to an enemy response that the group cannot safely absorb.

cards.heading: The campaign remembers a costly decision
cards.text: Characters gain experience through battle, allowing the army's strengths to develop over the campaign. Losing a unit can remove that individual from the remaining journey, giving an otherwise successful map a lasting cost. Recruiting and protecting people therefore matter alongside reaching the immediate objective. The Binding Blade uses the continuing roster to connect its separate battlefields: a capable veteran represents earlier decisions and successful encounters, while another recruit offers possibilities that still need to be developed. The larger strategy includes deciding whose growth can be supported without taking an unnecessary risk.

main.title: Armored Core 3
main.summary: Armored Core 3 is a 2002 third-person shooter video game developed by FromSoftware for the PlayStation 2.

cards.text: Armored Core 3 is a 2002 third-person shooter video game developed by FromSoftware for the PlayStation 2. It is the sixth entry in the Armored Core series. Armored Core 3 acts as a reboot for the franchise and begins a storyline that would continue through Armored Core: Last Raven. In 2009, Armored Core 3 was ported to the PlayStation Portable.

As a reboot of the franchise, Armored Core 3 returns to the post-apocalyptic world of the earlier PlayStation trilogy. The player is a mercenary in a future where humanity has been driven underground and is ruled by a powerful artificial intelligence called The Controller. Despite The Controller's rule, corporations fight each other for dominance.

Armored Core 3 is largely unchanged from its predecessor. Players operate mech units that they may customize with credits earned from completing missions and fighting in an arena. Customization extends to every aspect of a player's Armored Core unit, including the individual parts, weapons, paint, and emblem. Local multiplayer modes allow for up to 4 players to fight each other with their custom Armored Cores.

main.title: Lost Kingdoms
main.subtitle: FromSoftware · GameCube
main.summary: Lost Kingdoms is FromSoftware's GameCube action role-playing game about Princess Katia searching for her father as a black fog consumes the kingdom of Argwyll. A Runestone allows her to use magical cards that summon creatures and attacks. She cannot simply meet a monster with her own sword, so the deck supplies the means of surviving each encounter. The familiar idea of collecting fantasy creatures becomes an immediate physical problem: Katia must keep moving while choosing what to summon and where its effect will be most useful.

cards.heading: The princess carries a deck into the fog
cards.text: Lost Kingdoms is FromSoftware's GameCube action role-playing game about Princess Katia searching for her father as a black fog consumes the kingdom of Argwyll. A Runestone allows her to use magical cards that summon creatures and attacks. She cannot simply meet a monster with her own sword, so the deck supplies the means of surviving each encounter. The familiar idea of collecting fantasy creatures becomes an immediate physical problem: Katia must keep moving while choosing what to summon and where its effect will be most useful.

cards.heading: A card is an action in the surrounding space
cards.text: Battles unfold in real time, requiring attention to the character's position as well as the selected card. Different creatures and elemental relationships provide different answers to an opponent, making preparation important before the encounter begins. New cards can be found, purchased or created through changes to the collection. The player develops a deck whose contents should work together once danger closes in. A powerful summon is useful only if it can be deployed at a moment and place where Katia can survive long enough to benefit from it.

cards.heading: A different early FromSoftware adventure
cards.text: Kota Hoshino composed the music for a game released in 2002, with Activision publishing the overseas editions. A separate two-player mode lets opponents bring decks into direct competition under additional restrictions. Lost Kingdoms applies the studio's interest in dangerous fantasy environments to a particularly accessible central object: the hand of cards becomes the player's available response to the world. Its sequel followed in 2003, expanding a system that already made collecting and action closely dependent on one another rather than separate activities between battles.

main.title: The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind
main.subtitle: A newcomer learns Vvardenfell
main.summary: Bethesda released The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind for Windows in North America on May 1, 2002.

cards.heading: A newcomer learns Vvardenfell
cards.text: Bethesda released The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind for Windows in North America on May 1, 2002. Its island of Vvardenfell places a newcomer among giant mushrooms, shell architecture, temples and rival Great Houses. Players can follow the Nerevarine prophecy, join guilds or explore ruins, learning the region through conversations and travel. Written directions and geographical landmarks make finding a route part of that experience.

cards.heading: Architecture marks the Great Houses
cards.text: Silt striders, volcanic ash and unusual wildlife give Vvardenfell a distinctive landscape. The architecture of the Redoran, Hlaalu and Telvanni makes cultural and political differences visible between settlements. Arriving from outside gives the character a reason to learn these places and their alliances alongside the player. Its strange forms gradually become familiar points of orientation.

cards.heading: Reading routes in the landscape
cards.text: Quest directions describe roads, junctions, rocks and cardinal points. The journal preserves that information for the player to interpret during travel. A wrong turn can mean studying signs and silhouettes more closely on the next attempt. Over time, frequently travelled routes become recognisable, tying progress to a growing knowledge of the landscape.

cards.heading: Skills develop through use
cards.text: Using a weapon, casting spells, running or exercising another skill contributes to improving it. Character development therefore reflects repeated actions, including inefficient choices that a player may later reconsider. The system also permits deliberate repetition to optimise growth. Practice and calculation coexist in deciding what sort of character to build.
